regenerable_on: any guest running Plex Media Server with its API reachable, staged as harness/bin/se-capture-guest's plex case expects: SE_PLEX_URL and SE_PLEX_TOKEN in the capturing environment, forwarded to the guest and sent as the X-Plex-Token header. The server must be UNCLAIMED, which is what makes the placeholder token work — an unclaimed Plex answers its own subnet without authentication, which is how its setup wizard reaches it. Two libraries of different `type` with different non-zero item counts are needed or the ItemCount and Type anchors stop discriminating. Media can be anything ffmpeg will produce; the four files behind this capture are colour-bar clips with invented titles, matched by the personal-media agent so no metadata lookup leaves the guest.
anonymisation_note: Through BOTH halves of the gate. The manifest-driven walk (harness/scrub/plex.json) classified all 107 leaf paths across the five payloads and substituted FOUR — the server's friendlyName, its machineIdentifier, and the two library UUIDs — and the independent detectors, which share no pattern or code path with it, then found nothing in the committed bytes. The four are substituted because of what they ARE on every Plex rather than because this instance's were sensitive: friendlyName here was docker's random container hostname and machineIdentifier belonged to a VM that no longer exists, but both are the server's identity on a deployed instance, and classifying by kind is what makes the next capture safe by default. Two bounds are stated in the manifest rather than assumed: the library titles are Plex's own stock names over media this capture generated, and a session document — which names a WATCHER and what they were watching — is classified by nothing here and will be refused leaf by leaf, which is the right outcome.
note:
Captured from a server stood up for the purpose and DELIBERATELY UNCLAIMED. That is a property of the capture worth stating in the corpus rather than only in a commit message: no PLEX_CLAIM was ever passed, the config volume was empty at first boot so the server minted its own machineIdentifier, and the root document carries the server's own account state — `myPlexSigninState: none`, `myPlexSubscription: false`, and `claimed: false` on /identity. Those members are in the payload and a reader can check them.

Three collections from FIVE documents, and the fan-out is the thing a port gets wrong. `/library/sections` names the sections; each section then costs one more request to `/library/sections/<key>/all` with a zero-size container window, which is how a count is asked for without pulling the rows. So the number of documents is not fixed by the collector — it is 3 + one per section — and se-capture-guest captures them as ONE bundle for that reason: a section created or deleted between two ssh calls yields a capture whose totals name a section its own listing does not.

The sessions collection commits ZERO objects, and that is a reading rather than a gap. Nothing was playing, so the document is `{"MediaContainer": {"size": 0}}` with no `Metadata` member at all — an authoritative emptiness, which under batch authority RETIRES every session object a previous batch published. That is the correct behaviour for a session list and it is why the variant is worth having: a port that declined `unavailable` here instead of committing zero would leave stale sessions standing forever, and a port that crashed on the missing `Metadata` key would never commit at all.

The same document is read TWICE and by two different collections, which is the second thing to get right. `server` reads it for `SessionCount` — a number on the server row — and `sessions` reads it for the rows themselves. One request path, two collections, and a port that cached or that keyed the payload per-collection rather than per-path gets a 'not captured in this variant' from the replay seam.

Stated bounds, because a specimen shows one server on one day.

Nothing was playing, so `session_facts` is reached by no committed capture: the grandparent/title fold, the User, Player, State and TranscodeSession members, and the transcode decisions are all unvisited. That is the collection this subsystem exists to answer 'what is playing right now, and is it transcoding' with, and no corpus opens it. Capturing one means capturing a document that names a person and what they were watching, which the scrub manifest deliberately cannot classify.

`requests` is not here at all. It is seerr's collection, and seerr's first-run setup authenticates against a Plex ACCOUNT — the estate's account is exactly what a lab may not touch — so the collection is absent from the replay seam, from the live reference and from the comparator alike, and the gap is carried in corpus.NAMED_RESIDUALS rather than by this silence.

Both libraries answered their count, so `ItemCountUnobservable` is emitted by nothing, and the server answered, so `StatusUnobservable` and `ConfigMissing` are emitted by nothing. Three failure statements, no committed capture.

This server is unclaimed, so `myPlexSigninState` is `none`. A claimed server reports `ok` there and carries a subscription block; no fact reads either member, so the row is identical — but a reader should not conclude from this capture that the two are indistinguishable to Plex.
anchors_note:
Read off the five payloads by hand at staging, before any stream existed. The two timestamps were converted from their epoch seconds with the adapter's own usec_to_iso against the captured numbers, not copied out of a generated stream.

The objects are named `plex`, `1` and `3` because those are the rows' NATIVE names — the ids the adapter mints are `server:plex` and `library:<key>`, and the collator derives them from the declared prefix and the name, so an anchor on the id would assert the collator's work rather than the collector's. The library name being the section KEY and not its title is the point: `1` and `3` are not consecutive, because the TV library was created, deleted and recreated during staging, and a port that indexed sections positionally rather than by `key` produces `1` and `2` and fails both library anchors at once. That accident is worth keeping.

ItemCount 2 and 1 are the anchors that cost an extra request each, and they come from a DIFFERENT document than every other fact on the same row — `library-sections-<key>-all`, not `library-sections`. A port that read `size` instead of `totalSize` publishes 0 for both, because the zero-size container window means `size` is 0 by construction and `totalSize` is the answer; that is the single most likely way to be wrong here and both anchors catch it.

The two counts differ (2 and 1) on purpose. A port that fetched one section's count and reused it for every section satisfies an anchor set where both were equal.

Type `movie` and `show` differ for the same reason, and they are also the pair that proves the section list was read rather than assumed: both libraries hold video, and only the section's own `type` member distinguishes them.

Refreshing false is anchored as a BOOLEAN rather than omitted. `library_facts` publishes it `if raw.get('refreshing') is not None`, so a port that treated false as absent — the classic falsy test — drops the fact entirely and fails here, while a port that published the raw value satisfies it. This is the same shape as the null-versus-absent distinction traefik's noop@internal anchors catch, seen from the other side.

SessionCount 0 sits on the SERVER row and is anchored beside `sessions commit_objects 0`, which is the pair that separates the two collections reading one document. A port that let the sessions collection supply the server's count, or that published SessionCount only when non-zero, satisfies one and fails the other.

`sessions commit_objects 0` is the most important anchor in this variant. Zero committed objects is an authoritative emptiness that retires; a port that declined `unavailable` because the `Metadata` member is missing would emit no commit at all and fail here, which is exactly the absence-as-health failure this product is built against.

The three absences name three different failure statements, none of which this capture reaches. ConfigMissing would mean the receipts were incomplete — and under replay the token state is PINNED in the seam rather than read from the replaying machine's environment, so this anchor is what makes that pin load-bearing: unpinned, the adapter finds no SE_PLEX_TOKEN on whatever workstation is replaying and publishes `ConfigMissing: ['SE_PLEX_TOKEN']` from a variant whose payloads are the API answering. StatusUnobservable would mean the server went dark; ItemCountUnobservable would mean one section's count could not be read while the rest of its row stood.

Deliberately NOT anchored: `machineIdentifier`, `apiVersion`, `myPlexSigninState`, `ownerFeatures`, the thirty transcoder and capability booleans, the section `agent`, `scanner`, `language` and `Location` members, and `createdAt`. Every one is in the payloads and none reaches a row — a fact must be cited by an opinion, used in identity or a relation, or be part of the declared answer (DESIGN 15) — so anchoring one would assert something these collections do not publish. `machineIdentifier` in particular is the server's identity and would be a reasonable thing for a port's author to publish; that it is absent from every row is the design, and this note is where that is written down.
